55.0.s.en: (1) Fear and a cry for help

55.0.0.en: 1- “Give ear to my prayer, O God; and hide not thyself from my supplication.”

55.0.1.en: Hide not thyself: do not neglect and ignore.

55.0.2.en: David felt that he was in distress, so he asked God to listen attentively to his prayer and not to neglect his supplications, which are prayers made in lowliness and contrition before God. All this shows how much David felt his need of God, because he was in great distress.

55.1.0.en: 2- “Attend unto me, and hear me: I mourn in my complaint, and make a noise.”

55.1.2.en: 1- David faced severe distress, so that his heart was troubled and he did not know what to do. He hastened to God, lifted up his prayers, and asked Him for two things:

55.1.3.en: a- That He condescend and hear him, that is, that God lay aside His greatness and listen to lowly man, and this shows David’s humility.

55.1.4.en: b- That He answer him, because he has no deliverer but God, and this shows David’s faith and his need of God.

55.1.5.en: 2- David here is a type of Christ as He approached the Cross, when He was in the garden of Gethsemane and asked that the cup of suffering pass from Him. For He was in perplexity between His holiness and righteousness on the one hand, and on the other the necessity of bearing all the sins of the world upon His head.

55.2.0.en: 3- “Because of the voice of the enemy, because of the oppression of the wicked: for they cast iniquity upon me, and in wrath they hate me.”

55.2.1.en: 1- David explains that the voices of his enemies were raised against him with false accusations and rose up against him in anger, so they wronged him though he was innocent, whether his son Absalom, or his friend and counselor Ahithophel, in addition to his people whom David had shepherded, loved and defended for many long years. Thus they all rose up against him, drove him out and deposed him from his throne.

55.2.2.en: 2- David here is a type of Christ, against whom the priests and chief priests rose up, as did the scribes and Pharisees, and His traitor disciple Judas came forward and handed Him over to the priests, who tried Him in unjust trials and pressed Pilate to sentence Him to crucifixion.

55.3.0.en: 4- “My heart is sore pained within me: and the terrors of death are fallen upon me.”

55.3.1.en: David showed the extent of his suffering of pain, picturing his heart as a woman suffering the pains of childbirth, which are called travail. And as the woman expects her child, he expects a dreadful death for himself and for those around him, and he expresses these horrors as the terrors of death. That is, his feelings were in severe pain and in expectation of sudden troubles, for after his son turned against him, what was left to him? There is only God, his sole refuge.

55.4.0.en: 5- “Fearfulness and trembling are come upon me, and horror hath overwhelmed me.”

55.4.2.en: David continues to describe his feelings in his distress when he heard of Absalom’s turning against him. He said that fear covered him and surrounded him on every side, and also trembling, that is, intense fear, and horror, that is, violent agitation. All this shows the harshness of the trial, but in the midst of this intense pain God’s saving power toward David appears.

55.5.0.en: 6- “And I said, Oh that I had wings like a dove! for then would I fly away, and be at rest.”

55.5.1.en: 1- When evil surrounded David on every side, he wished that God would deliver him from it, and imagined that the solution was for God to give him the wings of a dove, so that he might fly and get away from this evil and be at rest. He chose the dove specifically because it signifies innocence, simplicity and forgiveness: even if doves quarrel with one another and strike one another with their beaks, they return after a little while and eat together in one love.

55.5.2.en: 2- Perhaps David, in the spirit of prophecy, saw the Holy Spirit, who appears in the form of a dove, and wished that God would give him the wings of the Holy Spirit to rise above the tribulations surrounding him. Even if he did not get away in his body, God would keep his spirit in peace in the midst of the severe tribulation, and he would be occupied with the love of God, and his heart would be filled with peace.

55.6.0.en: 7- “Lo, then would I wander far off, and remain in the wilderness. Selah.” 8- “I would hasten my escape from the windy storm and tempest.”

55.6.1.en: Tempest: a violent wind that causes disturbances in the sea.

55.6.2.en: 1- Before Absalom’s attack with many men to drive out and kill David, who in this represent the windy storm and tempest, David was forced to flee to the wilderness and lodge there. The barren wilderness is safer than the fortified city of Jerusalem, which was filled with evil because of Absalom, but in the wilderness and its quiet he sees God and rests in His hands.

55.6.3.en: 2- David used the words “lodge in the wilderness,” which means sleeping at the time of darkness, to express his severe distress and the blackness of his life, in his exposure to destruction at the hand of his son and the betrayal of his friend, but his hope and his stronghold is God.

55.6.4.en: 3- The spiritual man flees from the turmoil of the world and its violent currents to the wilderness, to be alone with God, to regain his peace, to feel God’s supporting power and to be satisfied with His love.

55.6.5.en: 4- He puts the word Selah at the end of verse 7; it is a musical pause in which man contemplates the importance of keeping away from evil and being alone with God.

55.6.6.en: 5- Christ would go out to the wilderness to pray and be alone, and so the monks through the ages left the world and devoted themselves to prayer in the deserts, and they supported the Church with their prayers, their love and their knowledge.

55.6.7.en: Do not deprive yourself of enjoying solitude with God, in which you contemplate His love and so praise Him and thank Him, and at the same time see your sins in the light of His love when you examine yourself, and so you repent with contrition, and God forgives you and purifies your heart.

55.7.0.en: 9- “Destroy, O Lord, and divide their tongues: for I have seen violence and strife in the city.”

55.7.1.en: Destroy: scatter their counsel, or make them confused.

55.7.2.en: 1- David felt the betrayal of Absalom, who began winning the people over to himself against his father David with lying words. David was moved and asked for God’s help to divide their opinions and scatter their counsel. He means Ahithophel, who had been David’s counselor and friend, and then turned against him and sided with Absalom.

55.7.3.en: 2- David saw violence spread in the city, that is, they wronged David, who was innocent, with false accusations spoken by Absalom, such as that his father David delayed justice in cases (2 Sam 15:2-4). He also saw strife in the city, for many turned against David and others defended him, so he asked God to calm the city and remove violence and evil.

55.7.4.en: 3- So also in the days of Christ, when the priests stirred up the people against Christ while some continued to praise Him because He worked miracles among them, Jerusalem was filled with strife and violence against Christ.

55.8.0.en: 10- “Day and night they go about it upon the walls thereof: mischief also and sorrow are in the midst of it.” 11- “Wickedness is in the midst thereof: deceit and guile depart not from her streets.”

55.8.1.en: The city of Jerusalem was filled with slanders against David, and they spread everywhere and surrounded all the people, and many of the leaders of the city fell into this plot and followed Absalom, and corruption spread in the city, even in its squares where the judges gather and show justice; all this was lost, and the squares became a place for stirring up the people against David with lies.

55.9.0.en: 12- “For it was not an enemy that reproached me; then I could have borne it: neither was it he that hated me that did magnify himself against me; then I would have hid myself from him:” 13- “But it was thou, a man mine equal, my guide, and mine acquaintance.” 14- “We took sweet counsel together, and walked unto the house of God in company.”

55.9.1.en: 1- David explains the extent of the distress that befell him, because the betrayal and the wrong came not from an enemy known for his enmity to David, but from a friend and companion who loved David, his counselor Ahithophel, whom David treated as a brother, not as a king with one of his servants, and David used to enjoy sitting with him, and sharing spiritual practices, whether ordinary visits to the house of God or at feasts and occasions. How then could betrayal, turning against him and lying come from this intimate friend? It is a thing of the greatest difficulty that wrongs should come to a man from where he does not know and does not expect.

55.9.2.en: 2- David said these words in the spirit of prophecy about Christ, who took Judas Iscariot as a disciple, even as a friend and companion, for He entrusted him with the money box and with arranging all the needs of Himself and the disciples, that is, He gave him a greater place among the disciples, yet he betrayed Him and handed Him over to the Jews to kill Him, and they crucified Him.

55.10.0.en: 15- “Let death seize upon them, and let them go down quick into hell: for wickedness is in their dwellings, and among them.”

55.10.1.en: 1- This is a prophecy from David about what would happen to Ahithophel, for he saw in the spirit of prophecy that death would take him by surprise and he would go down to Hades, where there is perpetual torment. Perhaps he was moved by the opening of the earth to swallow Korah, Dathan and Abiram and those with them (Num 16:32), and because Ahithophel persisted in evil and betrayed God and his master King David without cause. This actually happened: after David’s flight and Absalom’s seizure of the throne, with Ahithophel at his side, Absalom chose the counsel of Hushai and abandoned the counsel of Ahithophel, and Ahithophel was greatly distressed and in despair hanged himself (2 Sam 17:23).

55.10.2.en: 2- This is also a prophecy about Judas Iscariot, who, after handing Christ over to the priests, felt his sin, but in despair, and hanged himself (Mt 27:5).

55.10.3.en: Betrayal is very hard, and if it happened to you, you would be upset. So do not betray God by your sin, grieve Him and defy Him. How can evil come from you toward God, that is, from a son toward his father, and from a friend toward his friend? But there is hope: return and repent quickly, for He is tender and will forgive you, as if you had done nothing.

55.11.0.en: 16- “As for me, I will call upon God; and the LORD shall save me.” 17- “Evening, and morning, and at noon, will I pray, and cry aloud: and he shall hear my voice.”

55.11.1.en: 1- After David showed his distress at the bitter betrayal, the violence and the corruption that filled the city of Jerusalem through Absalom and Ahithophel, he took the right direction, that is, he turned to God in prayer. And because the pain of his heart was severe, he cried out. The greatness of David’s faith appears in his saying that the Lord will save him, for he trusts that his cry reaches God and that God will surely save him, though the salvation had not yet been accomplished and David had not returned to his throne.

55.11.2.en: 2- This cry began at the end of the day when David was alone with God in long prayer, which may have extended for hours during the night, and after sleeping a little he rose to continue his prayers in the morning and at noon, that is, throughout the day. He prays constant prayer by night and by day, and pours out all his feelings in complaint, weeping and appeal to God, who cannot turn away His children and those who seek Him.

55.11.3.en: 3- This is a prophecy about Christ, who in the depth of His suffering in the garden of Gethsemane cried out to the Father that this cup might pass from Him. And He was confident that He would save Him. This was accomplished: though He bore all the sufferings for mankind, and died, He rose on the third day. David, the type of Christ, bore in part the sufferings from his loved ones, but Christ bore all the sufferings, and truly died, and rose, to raise us in Him.

55.12.0.en: 18- “He hath delivered my soul in peace from the battle that was against me: for there were many with me.” 19- “God shall hear, and afflict them, even he that abideth of old. Selah. Because they have no changes, therefore they fear not God.”

55.12.1.en: 1- Absalom attacked with a mighty army gathered from all the tribes of Israel, that is, with a very great number, but David, who trusted in God, had his God intervene and redeem him and rescue him from the hand of Absalom, and Absalom died in his place, because God heard David’s cry and prayers, and humbled those who rose up against David, and they were defeated before David’s men. This is because those who rose up against David, that is, Absalom and Ahithophel, do not fear God and do not accept repentance and change; they are determined on evil, and therefore both perished: Ahithophel hanged himself and Absalom was killed in the war.

55.12.2.en: 2- The word Selah in (v. 19) is a musical pause, so that man may contemplate the power of God, who protects His children, and so keep away from evil and repent of his sins.

55.12.3.en: 3- The Jews stirred up the priests and asked Pilate to crucify Christ, but the Father heard Christ’s cry and delivered Him from death by His resurrection from the dead.

55.13.0.en: 20- “He hath put forth his hands against such as be at peace with him: he hath broken his covenant.”

55.13.1.en: 1- Here David spoke of the traitor Ahithophel, who cast upon David and all who were with him, who were at peace with him, the evil with which his hands were filled, and broke the covenant of love and friendship and his duty as counselor and servant to his master King David. These words apply also to Absalom, who rose up against his father who loved him and was at peace with him, broke the covenant of sonship, and wished to destroy his father.

55.13.2.en: 2- These words are also a prophecy about Judas Iscariot, who cast his evil upon the most important person who loved him, embraced him and made him a disciple, namely Christ, with whom he lived in peace for more than three years, and he broke the covenant of love and submission to his teacher. It is also a prophecy about the Jews who testified to Christ that He is a good teacher, and asked Him as a Savior to reign over their hearts when they received Him as He entered Jerusalem, for they rose up against Him, broke the covenant of love and demanded His crucifixion.

55.14.0.en: 21- “The words of his mouth were smoother than butter, but war was in his heart: his words were softer than oil, yet were they drawn swords.”

55.14.1.en: 1- Here David describes the hypocrisy and dissimulation of Ahithophel, and of Absalom. Ahithophel would show love as David’s counselor and friend, while his heart harbored evil against him and wished to destroy him. The verse likens his mouth to soft butter, but in truth he is a warrior, that is, one who destroys others, and likens him also to soft oil though in truth his words are drawn swords.

55.14.2.en: 2- These words are a prophecy about Judas Iscariot, who pretended to love the poor and objected to the pouring of the ointment on Christ’s head, though he intended to steal from the box in which the contributions given to Christ were put (Jn 12:6). And when he went to Christ in the garden of Gethsemane he kissed Him, so the kiss, which is a sign of love, became a means and a signal that Judas gave to the Jews so that they might seize Christ.

55.14.3.en: Do not show love to those around you while your heart harbors evil against them. And if you notice bad thoughts within you toward any person, hasten to repentance so that God may free you from them.

55.15.0.en: 22- “Cast thy burden upon the LORD, and he shall sustain thee: he shall never suffer the righteous to be moved.”

55.15.1.en: 1- If human beings are exposed to falling into betrayal, you will not find a son or a friend to depend on, and nothing will remain for you but God, on whom you trust and cast your cares, and He is sure to uphold you, provide for your needs and keep you.

55.15.2.en: 2- If God permits some tribulations for His righteous children, or if they sometimes fall into grave sins and repent, God will not leave them, but removes the tribulations from them, as He removed them from David and restored him to his throne. And if they have sinned like Peter and denied Christ, Christ rebukes them, forgives them and restores them to their first place.

55.16.0.en: 23- “But thou, O God, shalt bring them down into the pit of destruction: bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days; but I will trust in thee.”

55.16.1.en: 1- Everyone who walks in evil and does not live with God is exposed to two things:

55.16.2.en: a- He does not live out half his days, that is, he does not enjoy his life on earth in peace and joy with God; he has wronged his earthly life and filled it with misery and depression, even if he is immersed in material lusts.

55.16.3.en: b- His end is eternal torment, and so he loses his earthly and eternal life, because he walked in evil and held to it all his life.

55.16.4.en: 2- David affirms that he has chosen the better way for himself, which is trusting in God and enjoying fellowship with Him, so he lives secure and happy.

55.16.5.en: Remember Christ at the beginning of each day, and before any matter you enter into, to seek Him and cast your affairs upon Him, and you will enjoy His care, and this will move you to praise Him at all times.

55.16.6.en: The blessings of trusting in God. To the chief Musician upon the silent dove among strangers. A golden psalm (Michtam) of David, when the Philistines took him in Gath: “Be merciful unto me, O God: for man would swallow me up” (v. 1) Introduction:

55.16.8.en: 2- When was it written? When David fled from the face of Saul and was forced to go to the Philistine city of Gath, one of the five great cities of Philistia in ancient times. There he pretended to be mad, scrawling on the doors of the gate of the city and letting his spittle fall down upon his beard, and the king thought him mad and disregarded him (1 Sam 21:14).

55.16.9.en: 3- David expresses his distress, since he finds no place to hide from the face of Saul, so that he was even exposed to being seized by the enemy Philistines, and therefore he cries out to God, who is able to deliver him, because God delivers those who trust in Him. Therefore this psalm suits everyone who is exposed to severe tribulation and takes refuge in God to rescue him.

55.16.10.en: 4- There is a resemblance between this psalm and Psalm 34, because the title of both psalms shows that they were spoken in Gath, so they are alike in thanking God, who rescued David from his enemies, and in boasting in Him.

55.16.11.en: 5- It appears from the title of the psalm that it was said “upon the silent dove,” which is a quiet musical tune that suits the sorrowful words David felt and expressed.

55.16.12.en: 6- The title of the psalm also has “among strangers,” because David the prophet spoke it while he was a stranger among the enemy Philistines, but God kept him and delivered him from their hands, so he wrote this psalm to thank God and boast in Him.

55.16.13.en: 7- We find in the title of the psalm “a golden psalm (Michtam) of David,” and this means that this psalm is one of the important, distinguished psalms that David wrote, and some say that in ancient times they used to write it in gold ink.

55.16.14.en: 8- This psalm is a prophecy about the enemies who would meet the people of God in the days of the captivity, or afterward in the age of the Maccabees, when King Antiochus persecuted the people of God.

55.16.15.en: 9- This psalm was sung by the people on various occasions, especially when they passed through tribulation, so it is a liturgical psalm.

55.16.16.en: 10- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
